analysis.one_liner: Permanently repeals the federal estate tax, ending it retroactively for deaths after 2004.
analysis.headline: The bill to permanently repeal the estate tax was introduced by Sen. Jeff Sessions with 25 Republican cosponsors but never received a hearing or vote in the Senate Finance Committee before Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The 2001 tax law already phased the estate tax down and was scheduled to repeal it in 2010 for one year only, with the tax coming back in 2011. This bill would have made that repeal retroactive to 2005 and permanent, so no estate, gift, or generation-skipping transfer tax would ever apply again. Only the largest estates ever owe the estate tax, so the main effect is a large tax cut for very wealthy families, paid for by less federal revenue that other taxpayers or government programs must cover.
analysis.who_benefits: Families with estates large enough to owe the tax, and heirs of people who died after 2004, who would pay nothing instead of a 45-48% tax on amounts above roughly $1.5-2 million in exemptions. Tax lawyers, accountants, and insurers who sell estate-liquidity products would lose a major line of business.

how_it_helps.text: The bill moves the repeal date of the estate and generation-skipping transfer taxes back from 2010 to January 1, 2005, so it applies to deaths and transfers that already occurred after 2004 [S2][S3].
It removes the built-in 2011 expiration of the 2001 tax law's repeal, making permanent the repeal of taxes that today fall only on estates above roughly $1.5-2 million in exempt value [S2][S3].
It also strikes the gift-tax and generation-skipping provisions that would otherwise have revived in later years, ending the entire transfer-tax system rather than just the estate tax [S3].

analysis.who_pays: The federal government loses the revenue the estate tax raises each year, meaning other taxpayers would eventually pay more or receive fewer services. The tax currently falls only on the few largest estates, so the money is forgone specifically for heirs of the wealthiest families.

drawbacks.text: Repealing the estate tax permanently removes a dedicated revenue stream; the money not collected from the largest estates must be made up by other taxpayers or through lower government spending [S2][S3].

Making the repeal retroactive to 2005 means families whose members died in the interim would receive windfall refunds, and the 'sunset' structure of the 2001 tax law was left even more tangled, adding planning complexity in transition years [S3].

Because only estates above roughly $1.5-2 million in exempt value owed the tax at the time, nearly all of the benefit flows to the top few percent of estates, which is the strongest objection an honest skeptic of repeal would face [S2].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For the small number of families facing the tax, the benefit is large: no tax on inherited wealth above the exemption. For everyone else the bill is a net cost, since the revenue forgone from the largest estates would have to be replaced. The retroactivity to 2005 adds windfalls for estates of the recently deceased. On balance this is a targeted tax cut for concentrated wealth rather than a broadly shared benefit.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the Senate Finance Committee the day it was introduced and never received a hearing, a committee vote, or a floor vote before Congress ended.

narrative.text: Sen. Jeff Sessions introduced the bill on May 10, 2005, with 25 Republican cosponsors joining him at introduction [S3][S4].
The same day, the Senate read it twice and referred it to the Committee on Finance, which was its last action of any kind [S5].
No hearing, committee vote, or floor vote on S. 988 appears in its action history through the end of the 109th Congress [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Because the bill never moved, the estate tax stayed on the books and the federal treasury kept that revenue; heirs to the largest estates did not get the permanent repeal they were seeking.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Federal treasury kept the estate tax revenue

for.name: Sen. Jeff Sessions
for.what_they_did: Sponsored the bill to permanently repeal the estate and generation-skipping transfer taxes.

for.name: 25 Republican senators
for.role: Original cosponsors, including Ensign, Martinez, Cornyn, Hatch, Hutchison, Lott, and others

against.name: Senate Committee on Finance
against.role: Senate committee with jurisdiction over tax legislation, chaired by a Republican
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled a hearing, markup, or vote on the bill after it was referred; the bill died in committee.

sides.party_line_note: All 26 sponsors and cosponsors were Republicans; the bill's only recorded action was referral to committee, and no Democratic support appears in the record [S4][S5].

industries.industry: Heirs and owners of very large estates
industries.note: The bill permanently eliminates the only federal tax on inherited wealth above roughly $1.5-2 million, a benefit that flows almost entirely to the top few percent of estates. The forgone revenue would otherwise fall on other taxpayers or fund public programs.

industries.industry: Trust and estate planning industry (lawyers, accountants, insurers)
industries.note: Permanent repeal would erase much of the market for estate-tax planning and life-insurance products sold to cover estate tax liability. Their losing that business is tied to the public keeping the revenue.
